s1.title: Multiple choice — calculations and basic concepts

prim-add.title: Addition and subtraction
prim-add.subtitle: From small numbers to numbers up to 10 000
theory: We add and subtract place by place: first the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds.
Adding with regrouping: if the sum in one place is more than 9, carry one to the next place.
Subtracting with borrowing: if you don't have enough in one place, borrow 10 from the next place.

prim-mul.title: Multiplication
prim-mul.subtitle: Times tables and multiplying bigger numbers
theory: Multiplication is repeated addition: 4 × 3 = 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
Bigger numbers: break them apart — 23 × 4 = 20×4 + 3×4 = 80 + 12 = 92.
The order of the factors doesn't change the result: a × b = b × a.

prim-div.title: Division (with remainder)
prim-div.subtitle: Dividing evenly and dividing with a remainder
theory: Division shows how many equal groups a number is split into.
The relationship: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder.
The remainder is always smaller than the divisor. You can never divide by 0.

prim-ord.title: Order of operations
prim-ord.subtitle: Parentheses, then × and ÷, then + and −
theory: The correct order: 1) parentheses ( ); 2) multiplication and division (left→right); 3) addition and subtraction.
2 + 3 × 4 = 2 + 12 = 14 (multiplication first).
(2 + 3) × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20 (parentheses first).

prim-nec.title: Find the unknown number
prim-nec.subtitle: Simple equations with one unknown
theory: You find the unknown number by using the inverse operation.
x + a = b → x = b − a; x − a = b → x = b + a.
a × x = b → x = b ÷ a. Always check your answer at the end.

prim-num.title: Numbers: comparing, sequences, rounding
prim-num.subtitle: Natural numbers up to 1 000 000
theory: We compare numbers digit by digit, starting with the highest place value.
Rounding to the nearest ten: look at the ones digit (≥5 → round up).
Rounding to the nearest hundred/thousand: look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to.

prim-frac.title: Fractions
prim-frac.subtitle: Fraction of a number, adding, and comparing (fourth grade)
theory: A fraction a/b means a parts of a whole divided into b equal parts.
Fraction of a number: divide the number by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator.
With the same denominator: add the numerators; the fraction with the bigger numerator is the bigger one.

prim-mas.title: Units of measurement
prim-mas.subtitle: Length, mass, capacity, time, and money
theory: Length: 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm; 1 km = 1000 m.
Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g. Capacity: 1 l = 1000 ml.
Time: 1 hour = 60 minutes. Money: 1 leu = 100 bani.

The clock: the small hand shows the hour, and the big hand shows the minutes. When the big hand is on the 12, it is exactly on the hour. A week has 7 days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

prim-geo.title: Geometry: shapes, perimeter, area
prim-geo.subtitle: Geometric shapes, squares and rectangles
theory: Flat shapes: a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners; a square has 4 equal sides; a rectangle has 4 sides (two long, two short); a circle has no corners.
Perimeter = the length of the outline. Square with side l: P = 4 × l. Rectangle with length L and width l: P = 2 × (L + l).
Area of a rectangle = L × l; area of a square = l × l.
Length is measured in cm, area in cm².

prim-prob.title: Word problems
prim-prob.subtitle: Simple word problems (first grade) and word problems by method
theory: Bar model method: we draw bars/segments to see how the quantities are related.
Comparison method: we compare two situations and subtract to get rid of one quantity.
Unit method: first we find the value of a single unit.
Working backwards: we start from the result and do the inverse operations, in reverse order.

s1-ordinea.title: Order of operations
s1-ordinea.subtitle: Numerical calculations with parentheses and powers
theory: Order of operations: 1) parentheses and brackets ( ) [ ] { }; 2) powers and square roots; 3) multiplication and division (from left to right); 4) addition and subtraction (from left to right).
Example: 12 − 2 · 5 = 12 − 10 = 2 (multiplication first, then subtraction).
Watch out: follow the order — parentheses, powers, ×/÷, then +/−.

s1-procente.title: Percents
s1-procente.subtitle: p% of a number, price increases, and discounts
theory: To find p% of a number N, calculate N · p/100.
Price increase of p%: N + N·p/100. Discount of p%: N − N·p/100.
Watch out: p% of N = N·p/100 (not N − p).

s1-reale.title: Real numbers: opposite, absolute value
s1-reale.subtitle: The opposite, the absolute value, and types of numbers
theory: The opposite of a number a is −a. A number plus its opposite is 0: a + (−a) = 0.
The absolute value |a| is the distance from 0: |5| = 5, |−5| = 5.
Rational numbers can be written as fractions. Irrational numbers: e.g., √2, π (decimals that never end and never repeat).
Watch out: the absolute value is always ≥ 0; the opposite changes the sign.

s1-fractii.title: Decimals ↔ fractions
s1-fractii.subtitle: Conversions, including repeating decimals
theory: Terminating decimal: 1.2 = 12/10 = 6/5 (simplify).
Simple repeating decimal: 0.(a) = a/9. Example: 0.(3) = 3/9 = 1/3.
Watch out: to get the decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator.

s1-proportii.title: Proportions and simple equations
s1-proportii.subtitle: Finding the unknown
theory: In a proportion a/b = c/d, we have a·d = b·c (product of the extremes = product of the means).
A first-degree (linear) equation: isolate the unknown by moving the terms and dividing by the coefficient. Example: 2x + 3 = 11 → 2x = 8 → x = 4.
Watch out: in a proportion, you cross-multiply; you don't add.

s1-date.title: Reading data and averages
s1-date.subtitle: Charts, the mean, the median
theory: The mean (average) = (sum of the values) ÷ (number of values).
The median = the middle value after you put the values in order.
In a bar chart, the height of a bar shows the value.
Watch out: mean = sum ÷ number of values.

s1-elevi.title: Who is right? (square roots)
s1-elevi.subtitle: “Four students calculated…”: square roots, conjugates, powers
theory: Product of conjugates: (m + n√k)(m − n√k) = m² − n²·k (difference of squares), so the result no longer has a square root.
Taking factors out from under a square root: √18 = √(9 · 2) = 3√2; then combine only like radicals: 3√2 − √2 = 2√2.
Example: (5 + 2√6)(5 − 2√6) = 25 − 4 · 6 = 1, so the geometric mean of the two numbers is √1 = 1.
Watch out: (n√k)² = n² · k, not n · k; and the sign between the squares is a minus, not a plus (25 + 24 = 49 is the typical wrong answer).

s1-adevarat.title: True or false?
s1-adevarat.subtitle: Charts, practical reasoning, comparisons
theory: Check the statement with a quick calculation; if even one part doesn't match, the statement is false.
Bar chart: the height of a bar = how many students; “a score of at least 8” means the scores 8, 9, and 10.
Example: 3√5 = √45 and 2√11 = √44, so 3√5 > 2√11 (compare the numbers under the square roots).
Watch out: the interval [−2, 3] contains 6 integers (the endpoints count); a 10% price increase followed by a 10% price decrease does NOT bring back the original price.

s2-segmente.title: Segments and midpoints
s2-segmente.subtitle: Segment lengths, the midpoint of a segment
theory: The midpoint M of segment AB splits the segment into two equal parts: AM = MB = AB/2.
If the points are collinear in the order A, B, C, then AC = AB + BC.
Watch out: the midpoint cuts the segment in half; for collinear points, AC = AB + BC.

s2-unghiuri.title: Angles and parallel lines
s2-unghiuri.subtitle: Supplements, complements, corresponding angles, vertical angles
theory: Supplementary angles: they add up to 180°. Complementary angles: they add up to 90°.
When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding angles are equal, and so are alternate interior angles.
Vertical angles (formed by two intersecting lines) are equal.
Watch out: complement = 90° − angle; supplement = 180° − angle.

s2-triunghi.title: Triangles: angles, medians, areas
s2-triunghi.subtitle: Angle sum, centroid, area
theory: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
The centroid G divides each median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex (AG = 2/3·AD, GD = 1/3·AD).
Area of a triangle = (base · height) ÷ 2.
Watch out: area = base·height ÷ 2; the angles add up to 180°.

s2-paralelogram.title: Parallelograms: perimeter and area
s2-paralelogram.subtitle: Equal opposite sides, perimeter, area
theory: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal.
Perimeter = 2·(a + b), where a and b are the lengths of two adjacent sides.
Area = base · the height to that base.
Watch out: perimeter = 2(L+l); area = base·height.

s2-cerc.title: Circles: angles and radius
s2-cerc.subtitle: Central angle, inscribed angle, diameter
theory: An inscribed angle that intercepts the same arc as a central angle measures half of the central angle.
An inscribed angle subtended by a diameter (a semicircle) measures 90°.
Radius = diameter ÷ 2.
Watch out: circumference L = 2πr, area A = πr² (use the radius, squared for the area).

s2-corpuri.title: Solid figures: volume
s2-corpuri.subtitle: Cube, rectangular prism, pyramid, prism
theory: Volume of a cube = l³ (l = edge length). Volume of a rectangular prism = L · l · h (length · width · height).
Volume of a pyramid = (base area · height) ÷ 3.
Volume of a right prism = base area · height.
Watch out: volume of a cube = edge³.

s3-text.title: Word problems (systems)
s3-text.subtitle: Solved with equations / systems
theory: Use letters (x, y) for the unknowns, write the equations from the problem, and then solve the system by substitution or elimination.
At the end, check the solution against the problem.
Watch out: always check the solution against the problem.

s3-expresii.title: Algebraic expressions
s3-expresii.subtitle: Special product formulas
theory: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²;  (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) — difference of squares.
Spot the right formula and use it to calculate quickly.

s3-functii.title: Functions
s3-functii.subtitle: The linear function, its graph, intersections with the axes
theory: The graph of a linear function f(x) = ax + b is a straight line.
Intersection with the x-axis (Ox): solve f(x) = 0. Intersection with the y-axis (Oy): calculate f(0) = b.
To calculate f(x), replace x with the given value.

s3-cerc.title: Circles: chord, radius, Pythagoras
s3-cerc.subtitle: Radius perpendicular to a chord, circumference, area
theory: A radius perpendicular to a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord.
In the right triangle that is formed: radius² = distance² + (half the chord)² (the Pythagorean theorem).
Circumference of a circle: L = 2πr. Area of a circle: A = πr².

s3-paralelogram.title: Parallelograms and midsegments
s3-paralelogram.subtitle: Perimeter, area, midsegment
theory: Perimeter of a parallelogram = 2·(a + b). Area = base · height.
The midsegment of a triangle joins the midpoints of two sides and is equal to half of the third side.

s3-corpuri.title: Solid figures: surface area and volume
s3-corpuri.subtitle: Prism, cube, pyramid
theory: Right prism: lateral surface area = base perimeter · height; volume = base area · height.
Cube with edge l: total surface area = 6·l², volume = l³.
Pyramid: volume = (base area · height) ÷ 3.

en-ii3-11.statement: Triangle ABC has sides AB = 6 cm, BC = 7 cm and AC = 5 cm. Points M, N, P are the midpoints of sides BC, CA and AB, respectively. The perimeter of triangle MNP is:
hints: Each side of triangle MNP is a midsegment of triangle ABC.

hints: The diagonals divide the parallelogram into 4 triangles with equal areas.

en-ii4-03.statement: Rectangle ABCD has diagonal AC = 12 cm, and the acute angle formed by the diagonals measures 60°. The area of the rectangle is:
hints: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other: OA = OD.

solution: OA = OD = 6 cm and m(∠AOD) = 60° ⟹ AD = 6 cm.

hints: Draw the height CE ⊥ AB; EB = AB − CD.

en-ii4-05.statement: Trapezoid ABCD has bases AB and CD, and AB = 3 · CD. The midsegment of the trapezoid is 28 cm long. The length of the longer base AB is:

Let CD = x; then AB = 3x.

en-ii4-06.statement: Trapezoid ABCD has bases AB = 11 cm and CD = 3 cm. The length of the midsegment of the trapezoid is:
hints: The midsegment of a trapezoid is half the sum of the bases.

en-ii4-07.statement: Isosceles trapezoid ABCD has bases AB = 6 cm and CD = 3 cm, and AD = BC = 3 cm. The measure of angle ABC is:
hints: Connect the midpoint M of AB to C and D: you get three equilateral triangles.
All the angles can be found from 60°.
solution: With M the midpoint of AB: AM = MB = DC = 3 cm, and triangles AMD, DMC, and MBC are equilateral.
From this, m(∠ABC) = 60°, m(∠ADC) = 120°, m(∠CAB) = 30°, and m(∠ACB) = 90°.

en-ii4-08.statement: The diagonals of rectangle ABCD intersect at O, and m(∠AOB) = 84°. The measure of angle OAB is:
hints: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, so OA = OB.
Triangle AOB is isosceles.

en-ii4-09.statement: Rhombus ABCD has m(∠BAD) = 60° and diagonal BD = 12 cm. The perimeter of the rhombus is:
hints: Triangle ABD has AB = AD and a 60° angle.
So it is equilateral.
solution: AB = AD and m(∠A) = 60° ⟹ triangle ABD is equilateral, so AB = BD = 12 cm.

en-ii4-10.statement: Square ABCD has a perimeter of 16 cm. The length of diagonal AC is:
hints: Side = perimeter ÷ 4.

en-ii4-11.statement: Parallelogram ABCD has AB = 10 cm, diagonal AC = 24 cm, and AC ⊥ AB. The perimeter of the parallelogram is:
hints: Triangle BAC has a right angle at A.
BC = √(AB² + AC²).

en-ii4-12.statement: In parallelogram ABCD, N is the midpoint of side CD. The ratio of the area of triangle BCN to the area of the parallelogram is:
hints: Compare the base and height of the triangle with those of the parallelogram.
solution: A(BCD) = A(ABCD)/2, and BN is a median of triangle BCD, so A(BCN) = A(BCD)/2.

en-ii4-13.statement: Parallelogram ABCD has an area of 26 cm². Point M is any point on side BC. The area of triangle AMD is:
hints: The base AD of the triangle is a side of the parallelogram.
The height from M to AD is the height of the parallelogram, wherever M is on BC.
solution: BC ∥ AD, so the distance from M to AD is the height h of the parallelogram.

en-ii5-02.statement: Points A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, in that order, divide the circle with center O into 10 congruent arcs. The measure of angle AOC is:

en-ii5-03.statement: Segment AB is a diameter of the circle with center O, and C is a point on the circle such that m(∠CAB) = 52°. The measure of angle CBA is:

en-ii5-05.statement: From point P, outside the circle with center O and radius 8 cm, tangents PA and PB are drawn (A, B on the circle). If OP = 16 cm, then the measure of angle OPA is:
hints: The radius drawn to the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent.
In triangle OAP, the leg OA is half the hypotenuse OP.
solution: OA ⊥ PA and OA = OP/2 ⟹ m(∠OPA) = 30°, m(∠AOP) = 60°.
Similarly, m(∠OPB) = 30°, m(∠BOP) = 60°; so m(∠APB) = 60° and m(∠AOB) = 120°.

en-ii5-06.statement: Points A, B, C lie on the circle with center O, and m(∠ACB) = 77°, with O inside angle ACB. The measure of angle AOB is:
hints: A central angle is twice the inscribed angle that intercepts the same arc.
solution: Arc AB (the one inside the angle) measures 154°.

en-ii5-07.statement: Chord AB of a circle with center O and radius 7 cm subtends the central angle AOB, with m(∠AOB) = 120°. The length of chord AB is:
hints: Draw OM ⊥ AB: in triangle OMA, angle A measures 30°.
solution: OM ⊥ AB, m(∠AOM) = 60°, OM = 3.5 cm, AM = 3.5√3 cm.

en-ii5-08.statement: A circle with center O has a radius of 10 cm, and chord AB is 12 cm long. The distance from the center O to chord AB is:
hints: The perpendicular from the center to a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord.
Apply the Pythagorean theorem in triangle OMA.

hints: The central angle BOC measures 120°.

en-ii5-12.statement: Chord AB of the circle with center O is 9 cm long, and m(∠AOB) = 60°. The circumference of the circle is:
hints: Triangle OAB is isosceles with a 60° angle, so it is equilateral.
The radius is equal to the chord.
solution: OA = OB and m(∠AOB) = 60° ⟹ OA = AB = 9 cm.

en-ii5-13.statement: Square ABCD has a side length of 3√2 cm and is inscribed in the circle with center O. The circumference of the circle is:
hints: The diagonal of the inscribed square is a diameter of the circle.
Diagonal = side · √2.
solution: AC = 3√2 · √2 = 6 cm, so the radius is 3 cm.

en-ii6-02.statement: A right circular cone has a slant height of 13 cm and a height of 5 cm. The volume of the cone is:
hints: Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the base radius: r² = g² − h² (g = slant height).
V = πr²h ÷ 3.

en-ii6-03.statement: A regular triangular prism ABCA′B′C′ has a base edge of 4 cm and a height of 3 cm. The volume of the prism is:
hints: Base area (equilateral triangle) = l²√3/4.
V = base area · height.

en-ii6-04.statement: The sum of the lengths of all the edges of a cube is 60 cm. The volume of the cube is:
hints: A cube has 12 equal edges.
V = l³.

en-ii6-05.statement: The sum of the lengths of the edges of a cube is 72 cm. The total surface area of the cube is:
hints: A cube has 12 edges and 6 square faces.
A_t = 6l².

en-ii6-06.statement: All the edges of a regular square pyramid are 2 cm long. The lateral surface area of the pyramid is:
hints: The lateral faces are 4 equilateral triangles.
Area of an equilateral triangle = l²√3/4.

en-ii6-07.statement: A regular triangular prism has a base edge of 9 cm and a height of 12 cm. The lateral surface area of the prism is:
hints: The lateral faces are 3 rectangles.
A_l = perimeter of the base · height.

en-ii6-08.statement: The axial cross-section of a right circular cone is an equilateral triangle with a side length of 8 cm. The lateral surface area of the cone is:
hints: The slant height g equals the side of the triangle, and the diameter of the base also equals the side.
A_l = πrg.

en-ii6-09.statement: In cube ABCDA′B′C′D′ with an edge length of 9 cm, the measure of the angle between lines AB and B′C′ is:
hints: If the lines have no point in common, replace one of them with a parallel line through a point on the other.
B′C′ ∥ BC, and ABCD is a square.
solution: B′C′ ∥ BC, and AB ⊥ BC (an angle of square ABCD).
So the measure of the angle between lines AB and B′C′ is 90°.

en-ii6-10.statement: In cube ABCDA′B′C′D′ with an edge length of 6 cm, the measure of the angle between lines AB′ and AD′ is:
hints: Lines AB′ and AD′ have point A in common: join B′ to D′ and look at triangle AB′D′.
The face diagonals of the cube are all equal (l√2).
solution: All the sides of triangle AB′D′ are face diagonals (equal), so it is equilateral.
So the measure of the angle between lines AB′ and AD′ is 60°.

en-ii6-11.statement: In regular square pyramid VABCD, all the edges are 4 cm long. The measure of the angle between lines VA and DC is:
hints: The lateral faces are equilateral triangles.
For skew lines, use a parallel line (for example, AD ∥ BC, DC ∥ AB).
solution: DC ∥ AB, so the angle we want is ∠VAB, an angle of the equilateral face VAB.
So the measure of the angle between lines VA and DC is 60°.

en-ii6-12.statement: Cube ABCDA′B′C′D′ has an edge length of 7 cm. The length of diagonal AC′ is:
hints: Diagonal of a cube: d = l√3.

en-ii6-14.statement: A cube with an edge length of 8 cm is cut into 8 congruent small cubes. The edge length of one small cube is:
hints: The same number of small cubes fits along each edge of the big cube: k³ = 8.
solution: k³ = 8 ⟹ k = 2 small cubes along each edge.
Edge length of a small cube = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm.

en-ii6-15.statement: The sum of the lengths of all the edges of a regular tetrahedron is 36 cm. The length of one edge is:
hints: A tetrahedron has 4 vertices, 4 faces, and 6 edges.
solution: A regular tetrahedron has 6 equal edges.

s3t-apt1.statement: An apartment building has 3-room apartments and 5-room apartments. In total, the building has 18 apartments and 70 rooms. How many apartments of each kind are there?
hints: Let x = the number of 3-room apartments and y = the number of 5-room apartments.
solution: From the first equation: x = 18 − y. Substitute: 3(18 − y) + 5y = 70.
Answer: 10 apartments with 3 rooms and 8 with 5 rooms.

s3t-apt2.statement: An apartment building has 3-room apartments and 5-room apartments. There are 4 more 3-room apartments than 5-room apartments, and the building has 60 rooms in total. How many apartments of each kind are there?
hints: Let y = the number of 5-room apartments; then there are y + 4 apartments with 3 rooms.
solution: Answer: 10 apartments with 3 rooms and 6 with 5 rooms.

s3t-minge.statement: Several children are buying a ball together. If each of them gives 18 lei, they are still 30 lei short. If each of them gives 24 lei, there are 12 lei left over. How many children are there, and how much does the ball cost?
hints: The price: P = 18n + 30 and P = 24n − 12.
Set the two expressions equal to each other.
solution: Answer: 7 children; the ball costs 156 lei.

s3t-g01.statement: A student buys 10 notebooks, all at the same price, and has 32 lei left out of 62 lei. How much does one notebook cost?
hints: First find how much was spent: 62 − 32.
Then divide by the number of notebooks.

s3t-g02.statement: A number multiplied by 6 and then increased by 6 gives 174. Find the number.
hints: Write the equation 6·x + 6 = 174 and solve it.
Watch out: use inverse operations — first subtract 6, then divide by 6.

en-iii1-01.statement:
Sofia reads a book in three days. On the first day she reads 20% of the total number of pages, on the second day 25% of the remaining pages, and on the third day the last 144 pages.
a) Suppose the book had 260 pages. How many pages would be left for the third day? Is that possible?
b) How many pages does the book have?
hints: a) Calculate step by step: day 1, what is left, day 2, what is left.
b) Working backwards: the 144 pages make up 75% of what was left after the first day.
solution: a) Day 1: 20% of 260 = 52; 208 are left. Day 2: 25% of these; that leaves 156 pages ≠ 144, so it is not possible.
b) After the first day, x pages are left: 75% of x = 144 ⟹ x = 144 · 100 ÷ 75 = 192.

inputs.label: b) Number of pages in the book

en-iii1-02.statement:
Ilinca reads a book in three days. On the first day she reads 20% of the total number of pages, on the second day 50% of the remaining pages, and on the third day the last 148 pages.
a) Suppose the book had 390 pages. How many pages would be left for the third day? Is that possible?
b) How many pages does the book have?
hints: a) Calculate step by step: day 1, what is left, day 2, what is left.
b) Working backwards: the 148 pages make up 50% of what was left after the first day.
solution: a) Day 1: 20% of 390 = 78; 312 are left. Day 2: 50% of these; that leaves 156 pages ≠ 148, so it is not possible.
b) After the first day, x pages are left: 50% of x = 148 ⟹ x = 148 · 100 ÷ 50 = 296.

inputs.label: b) Number of pages in the book

en-iii1-03.statement:
A group of cyclists covers a route in three days. On the first day they cover 1/5 of the route, on the second day 1/2 of the remaining distance, and on the third day the last 48 km.
a) If the route were 130 km long, how many kilometers would be left for the third day?
b) How many kilometers long is the route?
hints: a) After the first day, 4/5 of the route is left; after the second day, 1/2 of that.
b) 48 km is 4/10 of the route.
solution: a) 130 · 4/5 · 1/2 = 52 km ≠ 48 km, so the route is not 130 km long.
b) Let T be the length of the route: T · 4/5 · 1/2 = 48.

en-iii1-04.statement:
The students of a class go into an assembly hall. If they sit 3 to a bench, 7 students are left standing. If they sit 4 to a bench, one bench stays empty and all the others are completely full.
a) If there were 13 benches in the hall, how many students would the class have, according to the first situation? Does that match the second situation?
b) How many benches are in the hall, and how many students are in the class?
hints: a) 3 · 13 + 7. In the second situation, 4 · (13 − 1) students would fit.
b) Let x be the number of benches: 3x + 7 = 4(x − 1).
solution: a) 3 · 13 + 7 = 46 students, but the second situation would give 4 · 12 = 48 students; it does not match.
Answer: a) 46; b) 11 benches and 40 students.

en-iii1-05.statement:
The students of a class want to buy a gift for their homeroom teacher. If each student gave 40 lei, they would be 20 lei short. If each one gave 45 lei, they would collect 120 lei more than the gift costs.
a) If there were 30 students in the class, how much would the gift cost, according to the first situation?
b) How many students are in the class, and how much does the gift cost?
hints: a) The price = 40 · 30 + 20.
b) The difference 45 − 40 = 5 lei per student covers 20 + 120 = 140 lei.
solution: a) 40 · 30 + 20 = 1220 lei; in the second situation we would get 45 · 30 − 120 = 1230 lei, so it does not match.
Answer: a) 1220 lei; b) 28 students, 1140 lei.

inputs.label: a) Price of the gift (with 30 students)

en-iii1-06.statement:
At a robot exhibition, 73 tickets were sold, some for adults (40 lei per ticket) and the rest for children (18 lei per ticket), bringing in a total of 1798 lei.
a) How many lei would have been collected if all the tickets had been for adults?
b) How many children's tickets were sold?
hints: b) Each children's ticket “replaced” with an adult ticket adds 22 lei. Compare with 1798.
solution: b) The difference: 2920 − 1798 = 1122 lei; a children's ticket is 22 lei cheaper.

en-iii1-07.statement:
An apartment building has 31 apartments, some with 2 rooms and the rest with 3 rooms. In total, the apartments have 68 rooms.
a) How many rooms would the building have if all the apartments had 2 rooms each?
b) How many apartments have 3 rooms?
hints: a) Multiply the number of apartments by 2.
b) Each 3-room apartment has one more room than assumed.
solution: Each 3-room apartment adds one extra room, so there are 6 such apartments.

en-iii1-08.statement:
The students of a school take part in a parade. If they line up in rows of 6, rows of 8, or rows of 10, there are 4 students left over every time. The number of students is a three-digit number.
a) Could there be 204 students? What is the remainder when 204 is divided by 6?
b) What is the smallest possible number of students?
hints: a) Divide 204 by 6; the remainder must be 4.
b) n − 4 is divisible by 6, 8, and 10, so by their LCM [6, 8, 10] = 120.
solution: a) 204 = 6 · 34 + 0; the remainder 0 ≠ 4, so there cannot be 204 students.
b) n − 4 is a common multiple of 6, 8, and 10; their LCM is [6, 8, 10] = 120.
n = 120k + 4; the smallest three-digit number of this form is 124.

en-iii1-09.statement:
The students of a school take part in a parade. If they line up in rows of 6, rows of 9, or rows of 12, there is one student left over every time. The number of students is a three-digit number.
a) Could there be 523 students? What is the remainder when 523 is divided by 12?
b) What is the smallest possible number of students?
hints: a) Divide 523 by 12; the remainder must be 1.
b) n − 1 is divisible by 6, 9, and 12, so by their LCM [6, 9, 12] = 36.
solution: a) 523 = 12 · 43 + 7; the remainder 7 ≠ 1, so there cannot be 523 students.
b) n − 1 is a common multiple of 6, 9, and 12; their LCM is [6, 9, 12] = 36.
n = 36k + 1; the smallest three-digit number of this form is 109.

en-iii1-10.statement:
Ioana and Matei have 292 lei together. If Ioana gave Matei 19 lei, the two of them would have equal amounts of money.
a) How many lei would each of them have after this transfer?
b) How many lei does Ioana have now?
hints: a) The total amount does not change with the transfer.
b) Right now, Ioana has 19 lei more than the amount from a).
solution: a) The total is still 292 lei, split equally: 292 ÷ 2 = 146 lei each.
b) After giving away 19 lei, Ioana has 146 lei, so right now she has 146 + 19 = 165 lei.

inputs.label: a) How many lei each has after the transfer
b) How many lei Ioana has now

en-iii1-11.statement:
Right now, the father's age is 5 times the son's age. In 3 years, the sum of their ages will be 48 years.
a) What is the sum of their ages now?
b) How old is the son now?
hints: a) In 3 years, each of the two will be 3 years older, so the sum grows by 6.
b) Let x be the son's age: x + 5x = the sum from a).
solution: The son is 7 years old, and the father is 35.

inputs.label: a) Sum of their ages now

en-iii1-12.statement:
The price of a pen is 25% of the price of a notebook. Mara buys 6 notebooks and 7 pens and pays 62 lei in total.
a) If a notebook cost 12 lei, how much would a pen cost?
b) How much does a notebook cost?
hints: b) Let x be the price of a notebook; a pen costs 25x/100. Write the equation for the total cost.

inputs.label: a) Price of a pen (notebook at 12 lei)

en-iii1-13.statement:
Three siblings, Vlad, Elena, and Teodora, share 330 lei. Vlad gets half of what the other two get together, and Elena gets 32 lei more than Teodora.
a) How many lei does Vlad get?
b) How many lei does Teodora get?
hints: a) If the other two get 2 parts, Vlad gets one part: 3 parts in total.
b) Elena + Teodora = 220, and Elena = Teodora + 32.
solution: b) Elena and Teodora get 330 − 110 = 220 lei together.
2 · Teodora + 32 = 220 ⟹ Teodora gets 94 lei (and Elena gets 126 lei).

inputs.label: a) How many lei Vlad gets
b) How many lei Teodora gets

en-iii1-14.statement:
Three friends have collected 73 stamps together. Alex has 14 more stamps than Bogdan, and Carla has 16 fewer stamps than Bogdan.
a) If Bogdan had 28 stamps, how many stamps would the three of them have in total?
b) How many stamps does Bogdan have?
hints: a) Alex: 28 + 14; Carla: 28 − 16.
b) Let x be the number of stamps Bogdan has: (x + 14) + x + (x − 16) = 73.
solution: a) (28 + 14) + 28 + (28 − 16) = 82 ≠ 73, so Bogdan does not have 28 stamps.

en-iii2-01.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x + 3)² − (x − 3)(x + 3) − 7, where x is a real number.
a) Write the expression in the form E(x) = mx + q and give the values of m and q.
b) Determine the largest integer x for which E(x) ≤ 80.
hints: a) (x + a)² = x² + 2ax + a², and (x − b)(x + b) = x² − b².
b) Solve the inequality 6x + 11 ≤ 80.

en-iii2-02.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (2x + 7)² − 4x(x + 1), where x is a real number.
a) Calculate E(−1).
b) Show that, for every natural number n, the number E(n) leaves the same remainder when divided by 24. What is this remainder?
hints: First, write the expression in simplified form.
solution: b) E(n) = 24n + 49; 24n is divisible by 24, and 49 = 24 · 2 + 1.
Answer: a) 25; b) the remainder is 1.

en-iii2-03.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x − 3)(x + 3) − 4(x − 2), where x is a real number.
a) Calculate E(0).
b) Determine the largest integer A such that E(x) ≥ A for every real number x.
hints: b) Write E(x) in the form (x − p)² + q.
solution: (x − 2)² ≥ 0, so E(x) ≥ −5, with equality when x = 2.

en-iii2-04.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² − 9)/(x² + 4x + 3), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−3, −1}.
a) Determine the number m for which x² + 4x + 3 = (x + 3)(x + m).
b) Determine the sum of all integers n for which E(n) is an integer.
hints: a) Look for two numbers whose product is 3 and whose sum is 4.
b) E(x) = (x − 3)/(x + 1) = 1 − 4/(x + 1); n + 1 must divide 4. Watch out for the excluded values!
solution: n + 1 must be an integer divisor of 4 (±1, ±2, ±4) ⟹ n ∈ {−5, −2, 0, 1, 3} (n = −3 is excluded: E is not defined there).

inputs.label: b) Sum of the values of n

en-iii2-05.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² − 16)/(x² + 5x + 4), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−4, −1}.
a) Determine the number m for which x² + 5x + 4 = (x + 4)(x + m).
b) Determine the sum of all integers n for which E(n) is an integer.
hints: a) Look for two numbers whose product is 4 and whose sum is 5.
b) E(x) = (x − 4)/(x + 1) = 1 − 5/(x + 1); n + 1 must divide 5. Watch out for the excluded values!
solution: n + 1 must be an integer divisor of 5 (±1, ±5) ⟹ n ∈ {−6, −2, 0, 4}.

inputs.label: b) Sum of the values of n

en-iii2-06.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² − 1)/(x² + 3x + 2), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−2, −1}.
a) Determine the number m for which x² + 3x + 2 = (x + 1)(x + m).
b) Determine the sum of all integers n for which E(n) is an integer.
hints: a) Look for two numbers whose product is 2 and whose sum is 3.
b) E(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 2) = 1 − 3/(x + 2); n + 2 must divide 3. Watch out for the excluded values!
solution: n + 2 must be an integer divisor of 3 (±1, ±3) ⟹ n ∈ {−5, −3, 1} (n = −1 is excluded: E is not defined there).

inputs.label: b) Sum of the values of n

en-iii2-07.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² + 2x + 1)/(x² + x), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−1, 0}.
a) Calculate E(5) + E(−5).
b) Calculate N = E(2) · E(3) · E(4) · … · E(17).
hints: Factor: x² + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)², x² + x = x(x + 1).
After simplifying, E(x) = (x + 1)/x; in the product, the numerator of each fraction cancels with the denominator of the next one.

en-iii2-08.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² − 1)/(x² − x), where x ∈ ℝ \ {0, 1}.
a) Calculate E(3) + E(−3).
b) Calculate N = E(4) · E(5) · E(6) · … · E(11).
hints: Factor: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), x² − x = x(x − 1).
After simplifying, E(x) = (x + 1)/x; in the product, the numerator of each fraction cancels with the denominator of the next one.

en-iii2-09.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² + 5x + 6)/(x² + 9x + 18), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−6, −3}.
a) Determine the number m for which x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 3)(x + m).
b) Determine the sum of the real solutions of the equation x · E(x) = 1.
hints: Simplify: E(x) = (x + 2)/(x + 6).
The equation becomes x(x + 2) = x + 6. Check that the solutions are in the domain!
solution: b) E(x) = (x + 2)/(x + 6); the equation becomes x² + x − 6 = 0, whose solutions are 2 and −3.
−3 is not in the domain (it makes a denominator zero), so it is discarded.
Sum of the solutions: 2. Answer: a) m = 2; b) 2.

en-iii2-10.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² + 3x − 10)/(x² + 11x + 30), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−6, −5}.
a) Determine the number m for which x² + 3x − 10 = (x + 5)(x + m).
b) Determine the sum of the real solutions of the equation x · E(x) = 2.
hints: Simplify: E(x) = (x − 2)/(x + 6).
The equation becomes x(x − 2) = 2(x + 6). Check that the solutions are in the domain!
solution: b) E(x) = (x − 2)/(x + 6); the equation becomes x² − 4x − 12 = 0, whose solutions are 6 and −2.
Both solutions are in the domain.
Sum of the solutions: 4. Answer: a) m = −2; b) 4.

en-iii2-11.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x/(x − 2) − 2/(x + 2)) · (x² − 4)/(x² + 4), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−2, 2}.
a) Calculate E(0).
b) Calculate S = E(3) + E(4) + … + E(8).
hints: Write the fractions with a common denominator: x/(x − 2) − 2/(x + 2) = (x² + 4)/(x² − 4).
Show that E(x) = 1 for every x in the domain.
solution: x(x + 2) − 2(x − 2) = x² + 4, so the expression in parentheses is (x² + 4)/(x² − 4).
a) E(0) = 1. b) S has 6 terms, each equal to 1, so S = 6.

en-iii2-12.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² − 25)/(x² + 10x + 25), where x is a real number, x ≠ −5.
a) Calculate E(35).
b) Determine the real number n for which E(n) = 1/6.
hints: E(x) = (x − 5)/(x + 5); in b), cross-multiply (the fundamental property of proportions).

en-iii2-13.statement:

b) Determine the real number n for which E(n) = 1/2.
hints: E(x) = (x − 2)/(x + 2); in b), cross-multiply (the fundamental property of proportions).

en-iii2-14.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x + 5)² − (x − 5)(x + 5) − 10, where x is a real number.
a) Write the expression in the form E(x) = mx + q and give the values of m and q.

b) Solve the inequality 10x + 40 ≤ 115.

en-iii2-15.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x + 5)² − (x − 4)(x + 4) − 12, where x is a real number.

en-iii2-16.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (2x + 4)² − 4x(x + 1), where x is a real number.
a) Calculate E(−1).
b) Show that, for every natural number n, the number E(n) leaves the same remainder when divided by 12. What is this remainder?
hints: First, write the expression in simplified form.
solution: b) E(n) = 12n + 16; 12n is divisible by 12, and 16 = 12 · 1 + 4.
Answer: a) 4; b) the remainder is 4.

en-iii2-17.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x − 6)(x + 6) − 4(x − 2), where x is a real number.
a) Calculate E(0).
b) Determine the largest integer A such that E(x) ≥ A for every real number x.
hints: b) Write E(x) in the form (x − p)² + q.
solution: (x − 2)² ≥ 0, so E(x) ≥ −32, with equality when x = 2.

en-iii2-18.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² + 5x + 6), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−3, −2}.
a) Determine the number m for which x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + m).
b) Determine the sum of all integers n for which E(n) is an integer.
hints: a) Look for two numbers whose product is 6 and whose sum is 5.
b) E(x) = (x − 2)/(x + 3) = 1 − 5/(x + 3); n + 3 must divide 5. Watch out for the excluded values!
solution: n + 3 must be an integer divisor of 5 (±1, ±5) ⟹ n ∈ {−8, −4, 2} (n = −2 is excluded: E is not defined there).

inputs.label: b) Sum of the values of n

en-iii2-19.statement:
Consider the expression E(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² + 3x + 2), where x ∈ ℝ \ {−2, −1}.

hints: a) Look for two numbers whose product is 2 and whose sum is 3.

solution: n + 1 must be an integer divisor of 3 (±1, ±3) ⟹ n ∈ {−4, 0, 2} (n = −2 is excluded: E is not defined there).

inputs.label: b) Sum of the values of n

en-iii2-20.statement:

en-iii3-02.statement:
Consider the function f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = −x/2 − 1.
a) Calculate f(−2) · f(2026).
b) The graph of the function f intersects the x-axis at point A and the y-axis at point B. Calculate the square of the distance from the origin O to the line AB.

d = OA · OB / AB (area computed in two ways), so d² = 4/5 = 0.8.

b) The graph of the function f intersects the x-axis at point A and the y-axis at point B. Calculate the square of the distance from the origin O to the line AB.

solution: a) f(4) = −4, f(−4) = 0; the difference is −4.
d = OA · OB / AB (area computed in two ways), so d² = 64/20 = 3.2.

M(6, 0), so AM = 12; the height from B is OB = 9.

en-iii3-05.statement:
Consider the function f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x/3 + 1.
a) Determine the real number m for which the point P(m, −1) lies on the graph of the function f.
b) The graph of the function f intersects the x-axis at point A and the y-axis at point B. Point M is the midpoint of segment AB. Calculate OM².
hints: a) P(m, −1) lies on the graph if f(m) = −1, that is, m/3 + 1 = −1.
solution: OM is the median to the hypotenuse: OM = AB/2, so OM² = 10/4 = 2.5.

en-iii3-06.statement:

en-iii3-19.statement:

s3c-3.statement: The area of a circle with a radius of 5 cm is of the form k·π cm². What is k?
hints: Area: A = πr².

en-iii5-01.statement:
Triangle ABC has a right angle at A, with AB = 8 cm and AC = 6 cm. Let AD ⊥ BC, with D on BC.
a) Calculate the length of the hypotenuse BC.
b) Calculate the length of the altitude AD.
hints: a) Use the Pythagorean theorem.
b) AD = AB · AC ÷ BC (area computed in two ways).
solution: b) AB · AC = BC · AD ⟹ 8 · 6 = 10 · AD.

en-iii5-02.statement:
Triangle ABC has a right angle at A, with AB = 18 cm and BC = 30 cm. Let D be the projection of point A onto BC.
a) Calculate the length of the leg AC.
b) Calculate the length of segment BD.
hints: a) AC² = BC² − AB².
b) The geometric mean (leg) theorem: AB² = BD · BC.

en-iii5-03.statement:
Triangle ABC has a right angle at A, with m(∠ACB) = 30° and AB = 4 cm.
a) Calculate the length of the hypotenuse BC.
b) The area of triangle ABC can be written as k√3 cm². Find k.
hints: a) The leg opposite the 30° angle is half the hypotenuse.
b) Find AC using the Pythagorean theorem, then the area = AB · AC ÷ 2.

en-iii5-04.statement:
Equilateral triangle ABC has a side length of 24 cm, and G is its centroid.
a) The altitude AM of the triangle can be written as m√3 cm. Find m.
b) The area of triangle GBC can be written as n√3 cm². Find n.
hints: a) The height of an equilateral triangle with side l: l√3/2.
b) GM = AM ÷ 3, and the area of GBC = BC · GM ÷ 2 (one third of the area of ABC).

inputs.label: b) n (area of GBC = n√3 cm²)

en-iii5-05.statement:
In the circle with center O and radius 10 cm, the diameters AB and CD are perpendicular, and M is the midpoint of segment OB.
a) Calculate the area of quadrilateral ACBD.
b) Calculate the area of triangle CMD.
hints: a) ACBD is a square whose diagonals are equal to the diameter.
b) In triangle CMD, the base CD is the diameter, and the height is OM.
solution: a) The diagonals of square ACBD are 20 cm long, so A = 20 · 20 ÷ 2 = 200 cm².
b) OM = 5 cm and OM ⊥ CD.

en-iii5-06.statement:
In a circle with center O and radius 13 cm, chord AB is 12 cm away from the center.
a) Calculate the length of chord AB.
b) Calculate the area of triangle OAB.
hints: a) OM ⊥ AB and M is the midpoint of the chord; use the Pythagorean theorem in triangle OMA.
b) Area = AB · OM ÷ 2.

en-iii5-07.statement:

b) Calculate the area of triangle OAB.
hints: a) OM ⊥ AB and M is the midpoint of the chord; use the Pythagorean theorem in triangle OMA.

en-iii5-08.statement:
Triangle ABC is inscribed in the circle with center O and radius 6 cm, side BC is a diameter, and m(∠ABC) = 30°.

b) The area of triangle ABC can be written as k√3 cm². Find k.
hints: BC is a diameter ⟹ angle A measures 90°.

solution: a) m(∠BAC) = 90°, BC = 12 cm, AC = BC ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

en-iii5-09.statement:

a) Calculate the length of the median AM.
b) Calculate the area of triangle GBC.
hints: a) The median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse.

en-iii5-10.statement:
Triangle ABC is isosceles, with AB = AC = 10 cm and BC = 12 cm. Let D be the midpoint of side BC.
a) Calculate the length of segment AD.
b) Calculate the distance from point B to the line AC.
hints: a) In the isosceles triangle, the median AD is also an altitude: use the Pythagorean theorem in triangle ADC.
b) Let BE ⊥ AC, with E on line AC. Area of triangle ABC = BC · AD ÷ 2 = AC · BE ÷ 2.

en-iii5-11.statement:
From point P, located 17 cm from the center O of a circle with a radius of 8 cm, tangents PA and PB are drawn to the circle (with A and B on the circle).

In isosceles trapezoid ABCD, the longer base is AB = 24 cm and AD = DC = CB = 12 cm.

en-iii4-17.statement:

solution: a) AECD is a rectangle ⟹ AE = 4 cm, EB = 8 − 4 = 4 cm; triangle CEB is an isosceles right triangle ⟹ CE = 4 cm = AD.

en-iii4-18.statement:
In isosceles trapezoid ABCD, the longer base is AB = 16 cm and AD = DC = CB = 8 cm.
a) Calculate the perimeter of the trapezoid.

hints: b) Draw the altitudes from D and C; the projections of the legs on the longer base each measure (AB − CD) ÷ 2.

en-iii4-19.statement:
Parallelogram ABCD has AB = 6 cm, AD = 7 cm, and m(∠DAB) = 30°.

en-iii4-20.statement:

en-iii4-21.statement:
Square ABCD has a side length of 9 cm, and M is the midpoint of side CD. Line AM intersects diagonal BD at point P.
